Every site using PHP can now safely upgrade their version to stay secure, in addition to applying mitigations from various security vendors.

Due to the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this bug to be one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory. It also marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact.

items.title: Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safe
items.content:
Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

items.title:
Is 10²⁵ FLOPs Still the Frontier?

A new Anthropic-written safety bill is circulating on Capitol Hill. Some of its ideas
items.content:
Is 10²⁵ FLOPs Still the Frontier?

A new Anthropic-written safety bill is circulating on Capitol Hill. Some of its ideas could be reasonable if limited to true frontier companies. As written, however, it will eventually sweep in most of Silicon Valley, damaging the startup ecosystem.

The bill defines the “frontier” as any model trained on 10²⁵ FLOPs — the EU standard from 2023. Biden’s executive order, California’s SB 53, and New York’s RAISE Act used 10²⁶ (ten times more). 10²⁷ is where the frontier actually is today (e.g., GPT-6 Astra).

Astra was reportedly trained on 100,000+ Grace Blackwell GPUs. A 10²⁵ model can be trained on as few as several hundred GB300 chips in three months. That is not frontier in 2026.

The definition is also cumulative: it adds FLOPs from fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other material modifications. In practice, that captures almost all meaningful post-training — work that is becoming commonplace in the enterprise.

The enterprise trend is toward thousands of smaller custom models built for specific workloads. These pose no frontier risk. Treating them as frontier systems would impose large compliance costs across corporate America for no safety gain.

Dario has claimed that Anthropic designs rules to disadvantage frontier companies like his own while advantaging smaller competitors. This definition does the opposite.

A stale 2023 cutoff favors incumbents who already clear the bar and can absorb the costs. It hobbles the open model ecosystem that threatens Anthropic’s pricing power. 

The frontier keeps moving. Any definition meant to track risk should move with it. 

Anthropic should clarify if they really believe 10²⁵ FLOPs represents the frontier.

items.title:
Sharing new post-training research on self-distillation + RL (JOLT), done together with @NVIDIAAI. 

In self-distillatio
items.content:
Sharing new post-training research on self-distillation + RL (JOLT), done together with @NVIDIAAI. 

In self-distillation, the same model performs the role of both a teacher and a student. The teacher gets extra information that the student doesn't, and the student learns from feedback provided by the teacher. However, the teacher could still use shortcuts in ways the student has no way to follow.

Our proposed approach, JOLT, trains the teacher as well, to learn from rewards on its own attempts, while penalizing any drift that's far off from what the student model would do. JOLT+ further supplements JOLT by providing the student model outcome-based rewards in addition to the teacher supervision signals.

On the MATH benchmark, we found that JOLT matches GRPO with 6.5x fewer training tokens, while JOLT+ convincingly beats GRPO across math, coding, terminal tasks, and tool use benchmarks.

items.title: In the '90s, general-purpose chips wiped out the specialists. The original Thinking Machines, Cray Computer, and a wave
items.content:
In the '90s, general-purpose chips wiped out the specialists. The original Thinking Machines, Cray Computer, and a wave of others shut down, and their best ideas got absorbed into other chips.

Zain Asgar of @gimletlabs argues the conditions that made generalists win have changed. Dennard scaling (shrinking transistors made chips faster at the same power) ended around 2005, transistor costs stopped falling around 2012, and memory bandwidth never kept up with compute.

Meanwhile, token demand is projected to grow 24x by 2030 while available power grows about 2x. When power is the bottleneck, performance per watt wins, and that's where specialized chips shine.

Full piece from Zain on why "the time of specialization is upon us": https://t.co/dFA8McPid5

items.title: The future of security in the AI age is "the constant pressure of models attacking you," says Kevin Mandia of @ArmadinSe
items.content:
The future of security in the AI age is "the constant pressure of models attacking you," says Kevin Mandia of @ArmadinSecurity. That means seeing your network the way a swarm of AI attackers would:

"We do a thing called a hyperattack. We throw a drone swarm of agents at you, and we map your network. Every service, every route, every system, all assets. We may end up with terabytes of metadata on your network."

"This is the attacker's view of your network. But with that metadata, we now just poll you almost like a heartbeat."

"What's changed?... Did a route change? Did a service get updated? Did a new machine get presented into the target area? We can poll cheaply for change and then attack the change."

"You can't [attack yourself] all the time because it's cost prohibitive, and it's unnecessary. You do it when either the threat changes, new models come out, new intelligence is available, or your network changes."

"Over the weekend, there was a zero-day in a popular product, and immediately we've already got the heartbeat. We just polled who's got the problem."

"Our goal at Armadin is to go from a known vulnerability to knowing whether it's actually exploitable before the bad guys can."

items.content:
AI models are getting close to designing hardware better than humans, and that shifts where the hard problems are:

- Better simulation, so physical builds become confirmation instead of experiments
- Demand shifts toward parts, machining and raw materials
- AI labs need to capture the "process knowledge" that lives in machinists and fabs

The one step even superhuman AI will struggle to speed up:

"A superhuman hardware engineer could design one million new iterations of the Apple Watch and get them manufactured for cheap, but then how can it know what customers actually want?"

But once AI crosses over, "the impact should prove immense: humanity will be able to directly use digital AI tools to bring about real, physical, material abundance."

Full piece from a16z's Christian Keil on what hardware engineering looks like once AI masters design: https://t.co/Mid6no8ozL

items.content:
Ekin Dogus Cubuk of @periodiclabs on why AI has to learn from the physical world, and building their own lab to close that loop:

"One of the more fundamental ways of making things around us is powder synthesis... You can actually, using that method, discover new superconductors, magnets, all kinds of materials that are very important for technologies around us."

"But at the core of it is just quantum mechanics. And we feel like teaching these LLMs quantum mechanics will be the next frontier for LLMs."

"Science is by its nature iterative, right? Like even the smartest humans tried many times before they discovered the things they discovered. LLMs can be very smart, but if they're not iterating on science, they won't discover science."

"The important thing to teach these LLMs is the method of scientific inquiry. So you do simulations, you do theoretical calculations, you do experiments, you get results, and the results are probably incorrect or not what you wanted at first, but you iterate on it."

"You have to do it with the real physics, not just the simulation."

@ekindogus @AnjneyMidha

a16z's Christian Keil makes the case for why building, testing, and iterating in the physical world is the bottleneck for AI in hardware: https://t.co/Mid6no8ozL

Adit Abraham of @reductoai on why everything in AI is "state-of-the-art all the time," and how to find what actually works for you:

"One of the unfortunate things about the AI industry... is benchmarks have become marketing over time."

"There's a public benchmark out there that we tested where if you take the same documents and you add a little bit of noise, like you tilt it one degree, you add a little Gaussian blur, the provider that published the benchmark gets way, way worse than everyone else, but everyone else is kind of consistent."

"Our recommendation is actually LLM as a judge is quite strong today if you're thoughtful about how you think about a rubric and how to approach it."

"We want to see the industry move closer to people testing on their own data, with tools maybe to make that evaluation easier."

"Instead of trusting a generic benchmark, you really should be at a point where you know what works best for you."

items.title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
items.content:
Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents Hey all, Kartik from Omnara (https://omnara.com) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API.

You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines.

Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada.

Here's some interesting architectural decisions we made while building this out:

Most harnesses, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, etc, run the agent loop in one long-lived process that keeps its log in a JSONL or SQLite file. In Omnara, the log is an append-only event log in Postgres, with inputs, model outputs and tool calls stored as typed rows in their own tables. The loop runs on stateless workers in the control plane. A worker runs one iteration of the loop, either a model call or the tool calls it produced, then releases the agent and puts the next iteration on a queue in Postgres. Whichever worker is free picks it up, so each iteration of an agent's loop can run in a different process on a different machine. Each iteration's result commits in one transaction, so the model output, its tool calls, usage and the next wakeup are saved together or not at all. If a worker dies mid-iteration, nothing commits, its lease expires, and another worker retries it. Agents waiting on a user, a tool or a retry don't hold a worker, so one worker can multiplex thousands of agents.

Also unlike other harnesses, the machines that the workers (our agent loop) run on aren't where the agent runs its commands. Instead, any macOS or Linux machine with an internet connection, like your laptop or any cloud sandbox, can run a small daemon (omnarad) that connects out to Omnara, so it doesn't need any open inbound ports. The agent then gets tools for that machine, like running a command or editing a file. An agent can have any number of machines connected to it. A fun thing I like to do is I have my laptop and a cloud sandbox connected to the same agent, so when my laptop is on, my agent codes there and I can interact with it, and I have it often push to Github. When I close my laptop, my agent sees the laptop went offline, pulls the latest changes to its cloud sandbox, and continues there.

The entire codebase is open source at https://github.com/omnara-ai/omnara, and it’s self hostable, even on a single machine with docker compose. You can also use the hosted version at https://omnara.com. Let me know what you think!

items.content:
Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents Hi HN! We’re Srikar and Kevan, founders of Alter – https://alterauth.com/. We’re building access control for agents that can take actions on behalf of multiple users.

If you’ve built an internal agent people use through Slack, you may have experienced this scenario: everyone signs in with their own account, but the agent connects to the CRM or billing system with one shared API key, so the agent can do anything that the key can do. User-level authentication in Slack does nothing to control what the agent can do in an external system like the CRM or billing system.

Here’s what Alter does:

-It acts as a proxy and manages downstream credentials for every API request that an agent takes;

-It takes identity into account for every action the agent does. Automatically take into account the end user identity of the person that the agent is taking actions on behalf of.

-It enforces fine grained runtime policies and records compliance grade audit logs.

Here’s a demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ZqPU14ipGE

We started this because we saw first hand how hard it is to build agents in regulated industries. To unlock the true benefits of agents we need to allow agents to take actions, sometimes actions on behalf of end users. I (Srikar) was working at Goldmans and I saw how prohibitively expensive it was for me as a developer to write my own custom auth to enable multi-tenancy in agents and to allow agents to have strict policy controls as they act on behalf of end users. My co-founder, Kevan, is a second time founder and was previously working on a database startup. He has experience building and selling deep tech into highly regulated environments. So this problem seemed like a natural fit for the both of us.

Building and maintaining custom auth for multi tenant agents was challenging. But so was ensuring that the solution we developed was secure, scalable and keeping track of security grade audit logs. As a result we realized there needs to be a separate product category for this that enables developers to easily build secure multi user agents that can actually take actions in an enterprise. Some of the real-world use cases we’ve seen include:

We have built a multi user open claw for our own team using Alter that saved us countless hours on our GTM effort. Link here:https://github.com/AlterAIDev/openclaw-alter-plugin

We have multiple startups who have used our platform to build their own secure internal agents for everything ranging from SRE agents to back office agents dealing with Quickbooks and payroll platforms like Rippling. It has saved developers countless hours both in terms of building and maintenance. We also have a defense contractor building air gapped agents for marine corp using Alter.

Under the hood, the value that we provide is that we do a lot of the plumbing that no one wants to do. We support hundreds of providers, all manually tested end to end. Reliability is our biggest priority. We have built this in a way to allow developers to custom build their agents however they see fit. Everything ranging from custom policies, agent delegation, user attribution, audit logs needed for compliance to a LLM gateway with guardrails (Coming soon)

Building a security product is hard. We have learnt that in order to build a truly secure product, security thinking has to pervade every part of the development process. We have embraced shift left security. Every PR that is pushed out is continuously checked for supply chain attacks, potentially dangerous code patterns etc.

Our business plan revolved around usage based pricing. There is a free tier up to 10k requests and then a pricing tier starting beyond that. We would love it if people configured their APIs and OAuth credentials, tried out the policies and actually built agents that can take actions with alter!

If you’ve built an agent that acts for multiple users, how are you handling permissions today? We’d especially like to hear what you’ve had to build yourself.

items.content:
BREAKING: OpenAI lost. Muse won.

Meta has the best AI agent - and no, I am not sponsored by Meta to tell you it's the best.

Enterpret launched Feedback Bench 1.1 (https://t.co/ZVgU2I7ypt), which ranks 9 personal AI agents using public posts from Reddit, X, YouTube, the App Store and the Play Store.

1/  The variables

☑ Popularity: how many people talk about the agent on socials. Hype is a good proxy for usefulness.

☑ Customer love: how users rate it compared with the other agents. 0.5 is the peer average.

☑ The heaviest-weighted area is “Getting tasks done” (~25%). Users care most about whether the agent is capable of doing things. I feel the same.

2/ The ranking

🥇 Muse (Meta)
🥈 Hermes Agent (Nous Research)
🥉 Grok Bot (xAI)

4. Hark (Hark Labs)
5. OpenClaw (OpenClaw Foundation)
6. Instinct (Spear Street)
7. Gemini Spark (Google)
8. ChatGPT Dots (OpenAI)
9. Poke (The Interaction Co.)

3/ Why using an AI agent vs. Claude/ChatGPT?

Technically, ChatGPT or Claude are "agents". People are getting ahead of themselves with this word. But Muse/Hermes/Grok Bot go an extra mile.

↳ They are using their own computer (not yours) to get things done. We call it "computer use" and it's useful to get things done on their own.

↳ You don't need to select their "intelligence". No more models or efforts to choose from.

↳ It's made for personal use cases. Do your taxes, book flights, shop online, fill out a form, etc.

PS: Claude just announced "Duet", their own personal agent. I will try to get early access; who wants to be in?

items.content:
if you've got a spare weekend and want to get better with Claude Code...

build these three projects:

1. your own "benchmarking" toolkit
- not those fancy dev tools, just prompts + systems + messy projects with tons of files
- run each new model through YOUR actual work
- you'll know within 15 minutes if it's worth switching
- saves 3 hours of reading other people's reviews that don't match your use case

2. a mini-saas for each repetitive task
- build something embarrassingly simple
- host it for $2/month, just for you, who cares about security anyway
- the goal is just to stop doing the same boring task manually

3. an AI assets library
- prompts, context files, MCPs, random github repos you might need
- sort them, make it easy to find, work on implementation guides
- when you need that one weird prompt at 3am, you'll find it in 30 seconds

these feel like side projects but it's actually the start of a decent infrastructure

items.content:
🚨 Your AI app is 9 layers deep.

And the LLM is only ONE of them.

Most people building with AI focus on the model.

But production AI is an entire stack 👇

1️⃣ LLMs — The brain
GPT-6, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek V4, Qwen3.8, Kimi K3

2️⃣ Inference & access — Where it runs
OpenRouter, Together, Fireworks, Ollama

3️⃣ Agent frameworks — The execution loop
LangGraph, Vercel AI SDK, Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK

4️⃣ Tools & protocols — How agents interact
MCP → tools
A2A → agent-to-agent communication

Claude Code vs Blender just exposed how AI can f*cking burn through your budget

Two workflows building the same complex 3D rocket assembly, but one ends up costing nearly 19x more in the demo

And the scary part is how easily those costs can spiral without improving the final result

Claude Code can reason through geometry, generate Python scripts, assemble mechanical components, and automate entire animation sequences

But every unnecessary tool call, failed generation, and repeated rebuild adds another layer of cost

Meanwhile, Blender can execute predefined operations without paying for another round of AI reasoning

Here’s where the workflows differ:

Traditional Blender:

MODEL individual rocket components
POSITION mechanical structures and hinges
CONFIGURE materials, lighting, and cameras
ANIMATE deployable panels
REFINE and reuse finished assets

Claude Code + Blender Python:

GENERATE geometry from written instructions
ASSEMBLE components programmatically
PARAMETERIZE dimensions and deployment angles
AUTOMATE animations and camera movements
REBUILD variations by modifying code

The real problem isn’t that AI is expensive

It’s using AI reasoning for work that a deterministic script could execute for almost nothing

Want to test the difference?

Open Claude Code with Blender installed and paste:

“Create a procedural Blender Python generator for a detailed rocket assembly with deployable panels, animated hinges, and realistic metallic materials

Separate geometry, materials, animation, and camera setup into reusable functions

Expose all major design parameters, reuse existing objects where possible, and track execution time and available AI usage costs”

The future isn’t Claude Code replacing Blender

It’s knowing when to stop paying AI to think and let specialized tools execute
